pages.text: Etse and Pearl’s class visited the Aburi Botanical Gardens in the Akuapem hills. The gardens were officially opened in March 1890, when Ghana was still the Gold Coast. ‘Where else could you meet so many kinds of trees in one morning?’ wrote Pearl.
sentences: Etse and Pearl’s class visited the Aburi Botanical Gardens in the Akuapem hills.
The gardens were officially opened in March 1890, when Ghana was still the Gold Coast.
‘Where else could you meet so many kinds of trees in one morning?’ wrote Pearl.
pages.alt: Children walk along a shady path in a hilly botanical garden.

pages.text: At the end of a path they found a tall tree with a bent, rusted label that nobody could read. ‘A tree with no name,’ said Etse. ‘That is a mystery.’ Mr Tandoh only asked: ‘What evidence could you collect without hurting the tree?’
sentences: At the end of a path they found a tall tree with a bent, rusted label that nobody could read.
‘A tree with no name,’ said Etse.
‘That is a mystery.’ Mr Tandoh only asked: ‘What evidence could you collect without hurting the tree?’
pages.alt: Two children look at a rusted, unreadable label beside a very tall tree.

pages.text: They became plant detectives. They sketched the leaves, which grew in groups of leaflets like the fingers of a hand. They drew the thick roots that spread like walls, and the fluffy white fibres drifting from open fruits on the ground. They picked nothing from the tree.
sentences: They became plant detectives.

They drew the thick roots that spread like walls, and the fluffy white fibres drifting from open fruits on the ground.
They picked nothing from the tree.
pages.alt: The children sketch leaves and wall-like roots, with white fibres on the ground.

pages.text: In a field guide, the pictures matched: Ceiba pentandra, the silk-cotton tree. In Twi it is often called onyina. Pearl’s grandmother in Ho used a different local name. ‘So one tree has many names,’ said Etse. ‘Which one is right?’
sentences: In a field guide, the pictures matched: Ceiba pentandra, the silk-cotton tree.
In Twi it is often called onyina.
Pearl’s grandmother in Ho used a different local name.
‘So one tree has many names,’ said Etse.
‘Which one is right?’
pages.alt: The children compare a field guide page with their sketches.

pages.text: Maame Ataa, a gardener, smiled. ‘All are right. Local names carry knowledge and stories. But scientists also give every species a two-part name, the same in every country, so a farmer in Ghana and a researcher in Brazil know they mean the same tree.’
sentences: Maame Ataa, a gardener, smiled.
‘All are right.
Local names carry knowledge and stories.
But scientists also give every species a two-part name, the same in every country, so a farmer in Ghana and a researcher in Brazil know they mean the same tree.’
pages.alt: A gardener in a sun hat talks to the children under the tree.

pages.text: Etse learned that a garden does more than grow pretty plants. It helps with research, conserves medicinal plants, multiplies plants for planting and trains people in horticulture. ‘It is a living library,’ said Pearl. ‘Each plant is a book we may not have read yet.’
sentences: Etse learned that a garden does more than grow pretty plants.
It helps with research, conserves medicinal plants, multiplies plants for planting and trains people in horticulture.
‘It is a living library,’ said Pearl.
‘Each plant is a book we may not have read yet.’
pages.alt: Pearl and Etse look at rows of plant beds with tiny labels.

pages.text: Pearl asked how herbalists’ knowledge is treated. ‘With respect,’ said Maame Ataa. ‘Healers share what they know, and researchers should ask permission, give credit and share the benefits.’ Pearl wrote it down. ‘Knowledge belongs to people too, not only to plants.’
sentences: Pearl asked how herbalists’ knowledge is treated.
‘With respect,’ said Maame Ataa.
‘Healers share what they know, and researchers should ask permission, give credit and share the benefits.’ Pearl wrote it down.
‘Knowledge belongs to people too, not only to plants.’
pages.alt: A gardener and children talk beside a bed of medicinal plants.

pages.text: Before they left, the class made a new label: a common name, a scientific name and the date. Etse added: ‘Identified by Primary 6 using leaf, root and fruit evidence.’ The tree had its name again, and the children had learned how names help us share knowledge. The end.

pages.alt: Children attach a new label to a post beside the tall tree.

activities.question: Which evidence did the children use to work out the tree’s identity?
options: Leaf shape, roots and fruit fibres
Only the colour of the bark

activities.prompt: The tree has several local names. Why might scientists also use one two-part name?
options: So everyone knows exactly which species is meant

activities.question: According to Maame Ataa, why do scientists give a two-part name to every species?
options: It is the same in every country, so everyone knows which species is meant
It is shorter than local names
